6.1.goal: Find out how surprising 60 heads in 100 flips would be if the coin were fair, first by simulation and then with the exact binomial test.

blocks.title: Set up the coin result
blocks.text: Our data: 60 heads in 100 flips. The null hypothesis says the coin is fair (chance of heads = 0.5). NumPy makes the pretend coins and SciPy gives the exact test.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

flips = 100
heads = 60
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)   # seeded, so the result repeats

print('observed:', heads, 'heads in', flips, 'flips')

blocks.title: Simulate a fair coin
blocks.text: We pretend the null is true and run 100,000 experiments of 100 fair flips. The p-value is the share of experiments at least as lopsided as ours, meaning 10 or more heads away from 50 in either direction.
blocks.code:
sim = rng.binomial(n=flips, p=0.5, size=100_000)   # heads in each pretend experiment
gap = abs(heads - 50)                              # our result is 10 away from 50
extreme = np.abs(sim - 50) >= gap                  # too many OR too few heads
p_sim = extreme.mean()

print(f'average heads in the simulation: {sim.mean():.2f}')
print(f'simulated p-value = {p_sim:.4f}')

blocks.title: Get the exact p-value
blocks.text: binomtest adds up the exact binomial chances, so no simulation is needed. The two-sided option counts both too many and too few heads. The simulated number should land close to the exact one.
blocks.code:
result = stats.binomtest(heads, n=flips, p=0.5, alternative='two-sided')
ci = result.proportion_ci(confidence_level=0.95)

print(f'exact p-value = {result.pvalue:.4f}')
print(f'95% CI for the heads rate: ({ci.low:.3f}, {ci.high:.3f})')

blocks.title: Make the decision
blocks.text: Compare p with alpha = 0.05 and word the result carefully. The normal-curve shortcut (z = 2) gives a smaller p, which would wrongly say 'significant'. This shows why the method matters when a result sits near the cut-off.
blocks.code:
alpha = 0.05
z = (heads - 50) / np.sqrt(flips * 0.5 * 0.5)
p_normal = 2 * stats.norm.sf(z)

print(f'normal shortcut: z = {z:.1f}, p = {p_normal:.4f}')
print('exact p <= alpha?', result.pvalue <= alpha)
if result.pvalue <= alpha:
    print('Reject H0: evidence the coin is not fair.')
else:
    print('Fail to reject H0: not enough evidence the coin is unfair.')

r.code:
binom.test(60, 100, p = 0.5)

# the simulation (random numbers, so close to but not exactly the Python value)
set.seed(42)
sim <- rbinom(100000, size = 100, prob = 0.5)
mean(abs(sim - 50) >= 10)
r.expect: p-value = 0.05689; 95 percent confidence interval: 0.4972 to 0.6967; sample estimate 0.6; simulated share about 0.057
r.note: binom.test gives the exact two-sided p-value and a 95% interval. The simulated share changes a little with every seed, so only the exact numbers must match.

spss.menu: Analyze > Nonparametric Tests > Legacy Dialogs > Binomial
spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / heads count.
BEGIN DATA
1 60
0 40
END DATA.
WEIGHT BY count.
NPAR TESTS

6.2.goal: Turn the bottling plant's z statistic into one-sided and two-sided p-values, and see what alpha = 0.05 means as a cut-off.

blocks.title: From the data to a z statistic
blocks.text: The plant claims bottles average 500 mL (sigma = 12 mL known). We weighed 64 bottles and got a mean of 503.6 mL. The z statistic says how many standard errors the sample mean sits from the claim.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

mu0, sigma, n, xbar = 500, 12, 64, 503.6

se = sigma / np.sqrt(n)
z = (xbar - mu0) / se

print(f'standard error = {se:.2f}')
print(f'z = {z:.2f}')

blocks.title: One-sided and two-sided p-values
blocks.text: norm.sf (the 'survival function') gives the area in the right tail beyond z. The two-sided p-value counts both tails, so it is double the one-sided value. A left tail uses norm.cdf.
blocks.code:
p_right = stats.norm.sf(z)         # area beyond +z
p_left = stats.norm.cdf(z)         # area below z
p_two = 2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(z))  # both tails

print(f'right-tailed p = {p_right:.4f}')
print(f'left-tailed p  = {p_left:.4f}')
print(f'two-tailed p   = {p_two:.4f}')

blocks.title: Alpha as a cut-off (critical values)
blocks.text: Alpha = 0.05 is the surprise threshold. norm.ppf turns it into critical z values that cut off the rejection region. Comparing |z| with the critical value gives the same decision as comparing p with alpha.
blocks.code:
alpha = 0.05
crit_two = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2)   # two-tailed cut-off
crit_right = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha)     # right-tailed cut-off

print(f'two-tailed critical z = +/-{crit_two:.3f}')
print(f'right-tailed critical z = {crit_right:.3f}')
print('p <= alpha?     ', p_two <= alpha)
print('|z| > critical?', abs(z) > crit_two)

blocks.title: Draw the tail areas
blocks.text: A picture of the p-value: the red areas are the two tails beyond +z and -z. Their combined area is the two-sided p-value, and they are tiny compared with the whole curve.
blocks.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(-4, 4, 400)
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.4))
plt.plot(x, stats.norm.pdf(x), color='black')
for side in (x >= abs(z), x <= -abs(z)):
    plt.fill_between(x[side], stats.norm.pdf(x[side]), color='tab:red', alpha=0.5)
plt.axvline(crit_two, linestyle='--', color='gray')
plt.axvline(-crit_two, linestyle='--', color='gray')
plt.title(f'z = {z:.2f}: two-sided p = {p_two:.4f} (red); dashed = critical values')
plt.xlabel('z')
plt.show()

r.code:
xbar <- 503.6; mu0 <- 500; sigma <- 12; n <- 64
z <- (xbar - mu0) / (sigma / sqrt(n))
z
pnorm(z, lower.tail = FALSE)   # right-tailed p
pnorm(z)                       # left-tailed p
2 * pnorm(-abs(z))             # two-tailed p
qnorm(c(0.975, 0.95))          # critical values
r.expect: z = 2.4; right-tailed p = 0.0082; left-tailed p = 0.9918; two-tailed p = 0.0164; critical values 1.960 and 1.645
r.note: pnorm gives the area to the left, so lower.tail = FALSE gives the right tail. qnorm is the inverse and returns the critical values.

spss.menu: Transform > Compute Variable (use the CDF.NORMAL and IDF.NORMAL functions)
spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / xbar mu0 sigma n.
BEGIN DATA
503.6 500 12 64
END DATA.
COMPUTE z = (xbar - mu0) / (sigma / SQRT(n)).
COMPUTE p_right = 1 - CDF.NORMAL(z, 0, 1).
COMPUTE p_left = CDF.NORMAL(z, 0, 1).
COMPUTE p_two = 2 * (1 - CDF.NORMAL(ABS(z), 0, 1)).
COMPUTE crit_two = IDF.NORMAL(0.975, 0, 1).
COMPUTE crit_right = IDF.NORMAL(0.95, 0, 1).
LIST.
spss.note: SPSS has no menu for a z-test with known sigma, so the numbers are computed with normal-curve functions. LIST prints z, the p-values and the critical values (shown with SPSS's default 2 decimals; double-click the output to see more).

stata.code:
display (503.6 - 500) / (12 / sqrt(64))
display 1 - normal(2.4)         // right-tailed p
display normal(2.4)             // left-tailed p
display 2 * (1 - normal(2.4))   // two-tailed p
display invnormal(0.975)        // two-tailed critical value
display invnormal(0.95)         // right-tailed critical value
stata.note: normal() is the area to the left of z and invnormal() is its inverse. The first line computes z = 2.4, which is then typed into the other lines.

6.3.goal: Simulate thousands of experiments to see the Type I error rate when nothing is going on and the power when a real 6-point effect exists, then check with a power calculator.

blocks.title: Plan the experiment
blocks.text: A teaching method may raise scores by 6 points (SD 15). We compare two groups of 36 students with a t-test at alpha = 0.05. The effect size d is the gap measured in SDs: 6 / 15 = 0.4.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n, sd, diff, alpha, reps = 36, 15, 6, 0.05, 10_000

d = diff / sd
print(f'effect size d = {d:.2f}')

blocks.title: Simulate when the null is true
blocks.text: We run 10,000 pretend experiments where both groups come from the same population. The share of experiments that still reject H0 is the Type I error rate, and it should be close to alpha.
blocks.code:
def reject_rate(true_diff):
    a = rng.normal(0, sd, size=(reps, n))
    b = rng.normal(true_diff, sd, size=(reps, n))
    p = stats.ttest_ind(a, b, axis=1).pvalue   # one t-test per row
    return (p <= alpha).mean()

type1 = reject_rate(0)
print(f'Type I error rate (no real effect) = {type1:.3f}')

blocks.title: Simulate when a real effect exists
blocks.text: Now the second group truly scores 6 points higher. The share of experiments that reject H0 is the power. With only 36 per group the test misses the effect more often than it finds it.
blocks.code:
power_sim = reject_rate(diff)

print(f'simulated power = {power_sim:.3f}')
print(f'simulated Type II error (beta) = {1 - power_sim:.3f}')

blocks.title: Check with statsmodels and plan the sample size
blocks.text: TTestIndPower does the calculation exactly, without simulation. power() gives the power for n = 36 per group, and solve_power() finds the group size needed for 80% power.
blocks.code:
from statsmodels.stats.power import TTestIndPower

analysis = TTestIndPower()
power_exact = analysis.power(effect_size=d, nobs1=n, alpha=alpha)
n_needed = analysis.solve_power(effect_size=d, power=0.80, alpha=alpha)

print(f'exact power with {n} per group = {power_exact:.3f}')
print(f'n per group for 80% power = {n_needed:.2f}, so use {int(np.ceil(n_needed))}')

r.code:
power.t.test(n = 36, delta = 6, sd = 15)                # power for 36 per group
power.t.test(power = 0.80, delta = 6, sd = 15)           # n per group for 80% power

# simulation (random, so close to but not exactly the Python value)
set.seed(42)
mean(replicate(10000, t.test(rnorm(36, 0, 15), rnorm(36, 0, 15))$p.value <= 0.05))
mean(replicate(10000, t.test(rnorm(36, 0, 15), rnorm(36, 6, 15))$p.value <= 0.05))
r.expect: power = 0.3875 for n = 36 per group; n = 99.08 per group for 80% power (use 100); simulated rates about 0.05 and about 0.39
r.note: power.t.test is exact for a two-sample, two-sided t-test, and n is per group. The two simulated rates change a little with every seed and will not match Python's digit for digit.

spss.menu: Analyze > Power Analysis > Means > Independent-Samples T Test (enter power 0.80 to solve for the sample size)
spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / n delta sd.
BEGIN DATA
36 6 15
END DATA.
COMPUTE df = 2 * n - 2.
COMPUTE nc = (delta / sd) * SQRT(n / 2).
COMPUTE tcrit = IDF.T(0.975, df).
COMPUTE power = 1 - NCDF.T(tcrit, df, nc) + NCDF.T(-tcrit, df, nc).
LIST power.
spss.note: The Power Analysis menu is the easy way and can also solve for n. The syntax shows the same exact power by hand, using the noncentral t distribution. SPSS has no built-in simulation here.

stata.code:
power twomeans 0 6, sd(15) n1(36) n2(36)      // power for 36 per group
power twomeans 0 6, sd(15) power(0.80)         // sample size for 80% power
stata.note: power twomeans takes the two group means (0 and 6) and the common SD. Stata reports whole group sizes, so it rounds the 99.08 up to 100 per group.

try: Change n to 100 and predict how the simulated and exact power change, then run it.
Change alpha to 0.01 and predict whether the power goes up or down, then run it.

6.4.goal: Run a z-test for a mean (the 50 bolts) and a z-test for a proportion (184 of 200 customers satisfied), by hand and with statsmodels.

blocks.title: A z-test for a mean, by hand
blocks.text: A line makes 10 mm bolts with a known SD of 0.5 mm. A sample of 50 bolts averages 10.14 mm. The z statistic is the gap divided by the standard error, and the two-sided p-value comes from the normal curve.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

mu0, sigma, n, xbar = 10, 0.5, 50, 10.14

se = sigma / np.sqrt(n)
z = (xbar - mu0) / se
p = 2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(z))
ci = (xbar - 1.96 * se, xbar + 1.96 * se)

print(f'z = {z:.3f}, p = {p:.4f}')
print(f'95% CI: ({ci[0]:.3f}, {ci[1]:.3f})')

blocks.title: The same test with ztest()
blocks.text: statsmodels needs raw data. We build 50 pretend bolt readings with mean 10.14 and SD 0.5, so the result matches the hand calculation. Note that ztest() estimates the SD from the data rather than using a known sigma.
blocks.code:
from statsmodels.stats.weightstats import ztest

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
x = rng.normal(size=50)
bolts = 10.14 + 0.5 * (x - x.mean()) / x.std(ddof=1)   # mean 10.14, SD 0.5

z_stat, p_val = ztest(bolts, value=10, alternative='two-sided')
print(f'mean = {bolts.mean():.2f}, sd = {bolts.std(ddof=1):.2f}')
print(f'z = {z_stat:.3f}, p = {p_val:.4f}')

blocks.title: A z-test for a proportion
blocks.text: A company claims 95% satisfaction, but 184 of 200 customers are satisfied. The claim says 'at least 95%', so we test the left tail ('smaller'). We set prop_var=0.95 so the standard error uses the claimed value, as a test should.
blocks.code:
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest

z_prop, p_prop = proportions_ztest(count=184, nobs=200, value=0.95,
                                   alternative='smaller', prop_var=0.95)

print(f'sample proportion = {184 / 200:.2f}')
print(f'z = {z_prop:.3f}')
print(f'left-tailed p = {p_prop:.4f}')
print('reject H0 at 0.05?', p_prop <= 0.05)

blocks.title: Why the standard error matters
blocks.text: If we leave out prop_var, statsmodels uses the observed 0.92 in the standard error. This is the classic mistake from the lesson, and it changes z and p.
blocks.code:
z_wrong, p_wrong = proportions_ztest(count=184, nobs=200, value=0.95,
                                     alternative='smaller')

print(f'with the observed proportion: z = {z_wrong:.3f}, p = {p_wrong:.4f}')
print(f'with the claimed 0.95:         z = {z_prop:.3f}, p = {p_prop:.4f}')

r.code:
# z-test for a mean (sigma known), by hand: base R has no z.test
z <- (10.14 - 10) / (0.5 / sqrt(50))
z
2 * pnorm(-abs(z))

# z-test for a proportion, no continuity correction
res <- prop.test(184, 200, p = 0.95, alternative = "less", correct = FALSE)
res
-sqrt(res$statistic)   # the z value (z squared is X-squared)
r.note: prop.test reports X-squared, which is z squared. For a one-sided test its p-value equals the z-test p-value, and correct = FALSE switches off the continuity correction so it matches.

spss.menu: Transform > Compute Variable (SPSS has no z-test menu; use the normal-curve functions)
spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / xbar mu0 sigma n x m p0.
BEGIN DATA
10.14 10 0.5 50 184 200 0.95
END DATA.
COMPUTE z_mean = (xbar - mu0) / (sigma / SQRT(n)).
COMPUTE p_mean = 2 * (1 - CDF.NORMAL(ABS(z_mean), 0, 1)).
COMPUTE z_prop = (x / m - p0) / SQRT(p0 * (1 - p0) / m).
COMPUTE p_prop = CDF.NORMAL(z_prop, 0, 1).
LIST z_mean p_mean z_prop p_prop.
spss.note: The first test uses the known sigma; the second is the left-tailed proportion test using p0 in the standard error. LIST shows 2 decimals by default; widen the columns in the output table to see more.

stata.code:
display (10.14 - 10) / (0.5 / sqrt(50))
display 2 * (1 - normal(1.9799))
prtesti 200 184 0.95, count
stata.note: Stata has no one-line z-test for a mean from summary numbers in older versions, so the first two lines work by hand. prtesti is the one-proportion z-test (it uses 0.95 in the standard error); read the Pr(Z < z) line for the left-tailed p-value.

6.5.goal: Check whether the average nitrate level in a river differs from the 3.2 mg/L guideline, using the lesson's nine readings.

blocks.title: Enter the data
blocks.text: Nine nitrate readings from one river, in mg/L, and the guideline value we want to compare against. NumPy holds the numbers and SciPy supplies the test.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

nitrate = np.array([3.1, 4.2, 2.8, 3.9, 4.5, 3.3, 4.1, 3.7, 3.5])
guideline = 3.2

print('readings:', len(nitrate))

blocks.title: Describe the sample
blocks.text: Always look at the numbers before testing them. The mean is the sample's centre, the standard deviation (ddof=1, the sample version) is its typical spread, and the standard error says how much a mean of 9 readings wobbles.
blocks.code:
mean = nitrate.mean()
sd = nitrate.std(ddof=1)
se = sd / np.sqrt(len(nitrate))

print(f'mean = {mean:.3f}')
print(f'sd   = {sd:.3f}')
print(f'se   = {se:.3f}')

blocks.title: Run the one-sample t-test
blocks.text: ttest_1samp asks: if the true average were exactly 3.2, how surprising is a sample mean this far away? It returns the t statistic (distance in standard errors) and the two-sided p-value.
blocks.code:
result = stats.ttest_1samp(nitrate, popmean=guideline)

print(f't  = {result.statistic:.3f}')
print(f'df = {len(nitrate) - 1}')
print(f'p  = {result.pvalue:.4f}')

blocks.title: Add a confidence interval
blocks.text: A 95% interval shows the range of true averages that fit the data. The guideline sits outside it, which agrees with the small p-value.
blocks.code:
ci = result.confidence_interval(confidence_level=0.95)

print(f'95% CI: ({ci.low:.3f}, {ci.high:.3f})')
print('guideline inside the interval?', ci.low <= guideline <= ci.high)

r.expect: t = 2.5866, df = 8, p-value = 0.03226; 95 percent confidence interval: 3.252 to 4.104; sample mean 3.678
r.note: t.test prints the t statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value and the 95% confidence interval together.

spss.menu: Analyze > Compare Means > One-Sample T Test
spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / nitrate.
BEGIN DATA
3.1 4.2 2.8 3.9 4.5 3.3 4.1 3.7 3.5
END DATA.
T-TEST
  /TESTVAL=3.2
  /VARIABLES=nitrate
  /CRITERIA=CI(.95).
spss.note: In the One-Sample Test table read t, df and Sig. (2-tailed); the confidence interval is for the difference from 3.2.

6.6.goal: Compare exam scores of 30 students who studied with music and 30 who studied in silence, with Welch's and the pooled two-sample t-test.

blocks.title: Enter the two groups
blocks.text: The scores below are built to match the lesson: music averages 74 (SD 8), silence averages 79 (SD 7), 30 students each. Different students are in each group, so the groups are independent.

blocks.title: Welch's t-test (the safe default)
blocks.text: equal_var=False gives Welch's test, which does not assume the two groups have the same spread. The degrees of freedom are not a whole number because they are adjusted for the unequal spreads.
blocks.code:
welch = stats.ttest_ind(music, silence, equal_var=False)

print(f't  = {welch.statistic:.3f}')
print(f'df = {welch.df:.1f}')
print(f'p  = {welch.pvalue:.4f}')

blocks.title: The pooled t-test
blocks.text: equal_var=True blends the two variances into one. Here the group sizes are equal and the spreads are similar, so the two tests agree closely. They would not agree if the smaller group were also the noisier one.
blocks.code:
pooled = stats.ttest_ind(music, silence, equal_var=True)

print(f't  = {pooled.statistic:.3f}')
print(f'df = {pooled.df:.0f}')
print(f'p  = {pooled.pvalue:.4f}')

blocks.title: Confidence interval for the difference
blocks.text: The test says whether the gap is real, and the interval says how big it might be. It is for music minus silence, so a fully negative interval means music scores are lower.
blocks.code:
ci = welch.confidence_interval(confidence_level=0.95)
diff = music.mean() - silence.mean()

print(f'difference (music - silence) = {diff:.2f}')
print(f'95% CI: ({ci.low:.2f}, {ci.high:.2f})')
print('interval contains 0?', ci.low <= 0 <= ci.high)

r.note: R's t.test uses Welch's test by default, so you must add var.equal = TRUE to get the pooled version. Both outputs also print the 95% confidence interval for the difference.

spss.menu: Analyze > Compare Means > Independent-Samples T Test
spss.note: SPSS prints both tests in one table: the 'Equal variances assumed' row is the pooled test and 'Equal variances not assumed' is Welch. Group 1 = music, group 2 = silence.

stata.code:
ttesti 30 74 8 30 79 7              // pooled (Stata's default)
ttesti 30 74 8 30 79 7, unequal     // Welch-type test, same df as R and Python
stata.note: ttesti runs the test from group size, mean and SD, so no data entry is needed (with raw data use: ttest score, by(group) and add unequal). Stata is pooled unless you add unequal. The lesson's rounded 74, 8, 79, 7 give t = -2.576, and Python's built data differ only in the 4th digit.

Cut each group to its first 10 scores (music[:10], silence[:10]) and predict whether the result stays significant.

6.7.goal: Test whether a drug lowers blood pressure in the lesson's 8 patients measured before and after, with a paired t-test.

blocks.title: Enter the paired data
blocks.text: Each patient appears in both lists, in the same order, so each 'after' belongs to a particular 'before'. The difference for each patient is their own change, and the lesson says every single one improved.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

before = np.array([142, 138, 155, 129, 147, 161, 133, 145])
after = np.array([135, 134, 148, 126, 139, 152, 130, 137])
diff = before - after

print('differences:', diff)
print(f'mean difference = {diff.mean():.3f}')
print(f'sd of differences = {diff.std(ddof=1):.3f}')

blocks.title: Run the paired t-test
blocks.text: ttest_rel compares before and after pair by pair. A positive t means the 'before' values were higher. We also add a 95% confidence interval for the average drop.
blocks.code:
paired = stats.ttest_rel(before, after)
ci = paired.confidence_interval(confidence_level=0.95)

print(f't  = {paired.statistic:.3f}')
print(f'df = {paired.df}')
print(f'p  = {paired.pvalue:.4f}')
print(f'95% CI for the drop: ({ci.low:.2f}, {ci.high:.2f})')

blocks.title: Same result as a one-sample test
blocks.text: A paired t-test is just a one-sample t-test on the differences, testing whether their mean is 0. The numbers come out exactly the same.
blocks.code:
one_sample = stats.ttest_1samp(diff, popmean=0)

print(f't  = {one_sample.statistic:.3f}')
print(f'p  = {one_sample.pvalue:.4f}')
print('same t as the paired test?', np.isclose(one_sample.statistic, paired.statistic))

blocks.title: What the wrong test says
blocks.text: If we ignore the pairing and treat the 16 numbers as two independent groups, the big differences between patients swamp the 6 mmHg drop. The result is far less convincing.
blocks.code:
wrong = stats.ttest_ind(before, after, equal_var=False)

print(f'independent test: t = {wrong.statistic:.2f}, p = {wrong.pvalue:.3f}')
print(f'paired test:      t = {paired.statistic:.2f}, p = {paired.pvalue:.4f}')

6.8.goal: Compute Cohen's d for the memory-training study by hand, then see a huge sample make a tiny effect significant while d stays tiny.

blocks.title: Enter the two groups
blocks.text: The memory-training study from the lesson: 25 people trained, 25 controls. The scores below are built to match the lesson (trained: mean 78, SD 10; control: mean 70, SD 12).

blocks.title: Cohen's d by hand
blocks.text: Cohen's d is the gap between the means measured in pooled standard deviations. The pooled SD is a weighted average of the two group SDs, so d does not depend on the sample size.
blocks.code:
n1, n2 = len(trained), len(control)
s1, s2 = trained.std(ddof=1), control.std(ddof=1)

sp = np.sqrt(((n1 - 1) * s1**2 + (n2 - 1) * s2**2) / (n1 + n2 - 2))
d = (trained.mean() - control.mean()) / sp
g = d * (1 - 3 / (4 * (n1 + n2 - 2) - 1))   # Hedges' g, a small-sample correction

print(f'pooled SD = {sp:.3f}')
print(f"Cohen's d = {d:.3f}")
print(f"Hedges' g = {g:.3f}")

blocks.title: Add the p-value
blocks.text: The t-test says whether the gap could be chance, while d says how big it is. Report both. (This is the pooled test; the lesson's Welch version gives the same p to three decimals.)
blocks.code:
res = stats.ttest_ind(trained, control)

print(f't = {res.statistic:.3f}, df = {res.df:.0f}, p = {res.pvalue:.4f}')

blocks.title: Tiny effect, huge sample
blocks.text: ttest_ind_from_stats runs the t-test from summary numbers. Compare three studies: a huge sample with a trivial gap, the memory study, and a tiny sample with a big gap. The p-values and d tell different stories.
blocks.code:
def study(label, diff, sd, n):
    res = stats.ttest_ind_from_stats(diff, sd, n, 0, sd, n)   # pooled test
    print(f'{label:<14} d = {diff / sd:.3f}  t = {res.statistic:.2f}  p = {res.pvalue:.4f}')

study('huge sample', 0.2, 15, 50000)
study('memory study', 8, sp, 25)
study('tiny sample', 15, 15, 4)

r.note: Base R has no Cohen's d command, so it is computed from the pooled SD. The helper function reproduces the huge-sample and tiny-sample studies (the memory study's t and p appear in the t.test output).

spss.menu: Analyze > Compare Means > Independent-Samples T Test (version 27 and later also prints an effect-size table with Cohen's d)
spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / label n diff sd.
BEGIN DATA
1 50000 0.2 15
2 25 8 11.0454
3 4 15 15
END DATA.
COMPUTE d = diff / sd.
COMPUTE t = diff / SQRT(2 * sd**2 / n).
COMPUTE p = 2 * CDF.T(-ABS(t), 2 * n - 2).
LIST label d t p.
spss.note: With raw data in two groups, the menu route above gives the t-test (and d in newer versions). The syntax shows the by-hand version for the three studies: 1 = huge sample, 2 = memory study, 3 = tiny sample. The pooled SD of the memory study (11.0454) comes from the lesson.

ttesti 50000 0.2 15 50000 0 15
stata.note: esizei takes each group's size, mean and SD and prints Cohen's d; ttesti runs the pooled t-test. With raw data use esize twosample score, by(group) cohensd.

6.9.goal: Compare incomes (in thousands) in two cities with 12 people each: check the t-test assumptions, then run both the t-test and the Mann-Whitney test and decide which to trust.

blocks.title: Enter and look at the data
blocks.text: Skewed incomes in two cities, 12 people each. Always look first: each city has one very large income, which pulls its mean far above its median.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

city_a = np.array([33.6, 26.6, 17.6, 64.6, 18.0, 23.9, 23.5, 23.2, 212.7, 39.8, 61.7, 59.1])
city_b = np.array([150.9, 42.3, 50.8, 36.2, 65.9, 95.3, 137.2, 45.7, 301.4, 50.7, 88.5, 63.9])

for name, g in [('A', city_a), ('B', city_b)]:
    print(f'city {name}: mean = {g.mean():.1f}, median = {np.median(g):.1f}, sd = {g.std(ddof=1):.1f}')

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.4))
plt.boxplot([city_a, city_b], tick_labels=['City A', 'City B'])
plt.ylabel('income (thousands)')
plt.show()

blocks.title: Check normality with Shapiro-Wilk
blocks.text: Shapiro-Wilk asks whether the data look like a sample from a normal curve. A p-value below 0.05 is evidence against normality. With only 12 per group, a normal-looking result would also not prove normality.
blocks.code:
for name, g in [('A', city_a), ('B', city_b)]:
    w = stats.shapiro(g)
    verdict = 'not normal' if w.pvalue < 0.05 else 'no clear problem'
    print(f'city {name}: W = {w.statistic:.3f}, p = {w.pvalue:.4f} ({verdict})')

blocks.title: Check equal spread with Levene
blocks.text: Levene's test asks whether the two groups have the same spread. We use the mean-centred version so it matches SPSS and Stata (SciPy's default centres on the median). A small p-value would mean unequal spreads.
blocks.code:
lev = stats.levene(city_a, city_b, center='mean')

print(f'Levene: statistic = {lev.statistic:.3f}, p = {lev.pvalue:.4f}')
print('spreads look equal?', lev.pvalue >= 0.05)

blocks.title: Run the t-test and Mann-Whitney
blocks.text: Welch's t-test compares means and is pulled around by the big incomes. The Mann-Whitney test uses ranks, so extreme values count only as 'the highest'. method='exact' gives an exact p-value when there are no ties.
blocks.code:
t_res = stats.ttest_ind(city_a, city_b, equal_var=False)
u_res = stats.mannwhitneyu(city_a, city_b, method='exact', alternative='two-sided')

print(f'Welch t-test:   t = {t_res.statistic:.3f}, p = {t_res.pvalue:.4f}')
print(f'Mann-Whitney:   U = {u_res.statistic:.1f}, p = {u_res.pvalue:.4f}')

blocks.title: Decide which to trust
blocks.text: Both groups failed the normality check and n is small, so the rank-based test is the safer choice here. The two tests disagree at alpha = 0.05, which is a warning that outliers matter. Say which test you chose and why, before looking at p.
blocks.code:
alpha = 0.05
print('t-test significant?      ', t_res.pvalue <= alpha)
print('Mann-Whitney significant?', u_res.pvalue <= alpha)
print()
print('Small, skewed samples: trust the Mann-Whitney result.')

r.code:
a <- c(33.6, 26.6, 17.6, 64.6, 18, 23.9, 23.5, 23.2, 212.7, 39.8, 61.7, 59.1)
b <- c(150.9, 42.3, 50.8, 36.2, 65.9, 95.3, 137.2, 45.7, 301.4, 50.7, 88.5, 63.9)
shapiro.test(a); shapiro.test(b)

income <- c(a, b); city <- factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = 12))
dev <- abs(income - ave(income, city))   # Levene = ANOVA on distances from the group mean
anova(lm(dev ~ city))

t.test(a, b)          # Welch
wilcox.test(a, b)     # Mann-Whitney (W equals U)
r.note: Base R has no Levene test, so the ANOVA on distances from each group mean reproduces it (its F equals Levene's statistic). Python's U and R's W are the same number, and both give the exact p-value when there are no ties.

spss.menu: Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Explore (Plots > Normality plots with tests); Analyze > Compare Means > Independent-Samples T Test; Analyze > Nonparametric Tests > Legacy Dialogs > 2 Independent Samples
spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / city income.
BEGIN DATA
1 33.6 1 26.6 1 17.6 1 64.6 1 18 1 23.9
1 23.5 1 23.2 1 212.7 1 39.8 1 61.7 1 59.1
2 150.9 2 42.3 2 50.8 2 36.2 2 65.9 2 95.3
2 137.2 2 45.7 2 301.4 2 50.7 2 88.5 2 63.9
END DATA.
EXAMINE VARIABLES=income BY city
  /PLOT=NPPLOT.
T-TEST GROUPS=city(1 2)
  /VARIABLES=income.
NPAR TESTS
  /M-W=income BY city(1 2).
spss.note: EXAMINE prints the Shapiro-Wilk test per city. The t-test table includes Levene's test (mean-based, matching Python above) and both t rows; read the 'not assumed' row for Welch. In the Mann-Whitney table use the Exact Sig. (2-tailed) line.

stata.code:
clear
set obs 24
generate city = 1 + (_n > 12)
generate income = real(word("33.6 26.6 17.6 64.6 18 23.9 23.5 23.2 212.7 39.8 61.7 59.1 150.9 42.3 50.8 36.2 65.9 95.3 137.2 45.7 301.4 50.7 88.5 63.9", _n))
swilk income if city == 1
swilk income if city == 2
robvar income, by(city)
ttest income, by(city) unequal
ranksum income, by(city)
stata.note: word() picks the nth number from the text so the 24 values fit in one line. robvar prints three versions of Levene's test; use W0 (mean-based). Stata's ttest is pooled unless you add unequal. ranksum reports a z-based p, and an exact p-value too for small samples.
